```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

A family usually has several maximum sets, all equally large. Covariates can decide among
them in two ways: by preferring some individuals within each family
(`rkn_select_criteria()`), or by steering the composition of the whole selection towards a
target proportion or mean (`rkn_select_global()`). This vignette uses the example cohort,
with the network built as in *Get started with RedKinNet*.

```{r}
library(RedKinNet)
kin <- rkn_example$kinship
covariates <- rkn_example$samples
chk <- rkn_check_samples(kin, threshold = "third", samples = covariates$id)
g <- rkn_graph_from_kinship(kin, threshold = "third", samples = covariates$id,
                            exclude = chk$contamination$id, covariates = covariates,
                            check = FALSE)
```

## Preferring individuals

A criterion states a preference: `rkn_criterion_cutoff()` prefers values above or below a
cutoff, and `rkn_criterion_level()` prefers one value of a covariate, such as cases over
controls. Here the samples with a call rate above 0.99, the better-genotyped ones, are
preferred whenever the family offers a choice.

```{r}
prefer_quality <- rkn_criterion_cutoff("call_rate", cutoff = 0.99, prefer = "above")
sel <- rkn_select_criteria(g, prefer_quality, seed = 1)
sel
```

By default the criteria decide the choices left open by the structural rules. With
`optimal = TRUE` they choose among all the maximum sets of each family, so that the
selection contains as many preferred individuals as possible.

```{r}
sel_optimal <- rkn_select_criteria(g, prefer_quality, optimal = TRUE, seed = 1)
low_quality <- function(s) sum(covariates$call_rate[match(s$kept, covariates$id)] <= 0.99)
c(default = low_quality(sel), optimal = low_quality(sel_optimal),
  uniform = low_quality(rkn_select_random(g, uniform = TRUE, seed = 1)))
```

A second criterion breaks the ties left by the first, for instance preferring older
individuals when the call rate does not decide.

```{r}
prefer_older <- rkn_criterion_cutoff("age", cutoff = 50, prefer = "above")
rkn_select_criteria(g, prefer_quality, prefer_older, optimal = TRUE, seed = 1)
```

Since every family keeps its largest size, a preference applied within each family is also
best for the selection as a whole: no choice in one family can make up for another.

## A target composition

Some targets concern the selection as a whole: as many women as men, or a mean age matching
that of a group of cases. The best choice in one family then depends on the others, and
`rkn_select_global()` chooses all the families jointly, exactly.

```{r}
balanced <- rkn_select_global(g, "sex", target = c(F = 0.5), seed = 1)
balanced
```

Without a target, the selection keeps the composition of the cohort.

```{r}
rkn_select_global(g, "sex", seed = 1)
```

For a numeric covariate the target is a mean. The values are rounded to a grid for the
search, whose step is the `resolution`; the reported mean is that of the recorded values.
A family whose computation would exceed the time and memory budget is resolved
approximately, and the printed summary says so; a coarser resolution makes the computation
smaller.

```{r}
rkn_select_global(g, "age", target = 50, seed = 1)
rkn_select_global(g, "age", target = 50, resolution = 5, seed = 1)
```

## Giving up individuals for a closer composition

The selections of the largest size reach a range of compositions, and a target outside that
range cannot be met without giving up individuals. `rkn_tradeoff()` shows, before
selecting, the composition reachable for each number of individuals given up.

```{r}
tr <- rkn_tradeoff(g, "sex", target = c(F = 0.65))
tr
```

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
plot(tr)
```

The argument `max_loss` of `rkn_select_global()` then allows that many individuals to be
given up.

```{r}
rkn_select_global(g, "sex", target = c(F = 0.65), max_loss = attr(tr, "tradeoff")$reached, seed = 1)
```
